title: The Middle Children
question: Logarithmically, humans sit roughly midway between atoms (~10^-10 m) and the observable universe (~10^26 m) — about 10^36 separates us from each end.
correctExplanation: True. Mid-scale creatures: ~16 orders above atoms, ~26 below the cosmic edge — middle children of magnitude. Powers of ten humble both directions.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Count zeros: atoms at 10^-10, people near 10^0, cosmos at 10^26. We split the difference surprisingly evenly — medium is our address.
lessonContent:
Powers of ten humble both directions.
Medium is humanity's true address.
Zeros counted beat intuitions felt.
Middle children span 36 orders.
Share this: place yourself logarithmically.

title: The Ninety-Three Billion
question: Because space itself expanded while ancient light traveled, the observable universe spans roughly 93 billion light-years across — far wider than its 13.8-billion-year age suggests.
correctExplanation: True. Expansion stretched the journey: sources now 46 billion light-years away emitted what arrives today. Age times lightspeed undershoots badly.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Distant galaxies receded during their light's travel: proper distances today dwarf light-travel distances. Thirteen-eight billion years, ninety-three billion light-years — expansion explains the gap.
lessonContent:
Expansion stretches journeys enormously.
Ages undershoot diameters badly here.
Proper distances dwarf travel distances.
Space itself does the extra miles.
Share this: span 93 billion light-years.

title: The Thirteen-Eight Width
question: Since the universe is 13.8 billion years old, its observable diameter must be exactly 13.8 billion light-years — nothing outruns light.
correctExplanation: False. Light-speed limits travel, not separation: expansion carries galaxies apart faster than light crosses. Diameter runs ~93 billion light-years.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Nothing outruns light locally, yet space itself stretches: recession velocities exceed c legitimately. Age-times-c is the rookie error cosmology corrects.
lessonContent:
Expansion outruns light legitimately.
Local limits never bind global stretch.
Rookie errors multiply age by c.
Diameters dwarf ages sevenfold here.
Share this: unbind one cosmic speed.

title: The Sandy Cosmos
question: Some claim beach sand grains outnumber all stars in the observable universe. In fact the stars win enormously: ~10^22-24 versus ~10^18-20 grains.
correctExplanation: False as stated — the claim reverses reality: stars outnumber sand grains by thousands. Sagan's original point flattered the cosmos, not the beach.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Count: observable stars ~10^23, beach grains ~10^19. The famous comparison runs stars-over-sand; reversing it breaks the orders.
lessonContent:
Reversed comparisons break orders badly.
Stars outnumber grains by thousands.
Famous ratios run one direction only.
Count zeros before quoting Sagan.
Share this: outcount one beach tonight.

title: The Glass Ocean
question: A single glass of water holds more molecules (~10^25) than there are glassfuls of water in all Earth's oceans (~10^22).
correctExplanation: True. Molecules per glass dwarf glasses per ocean by a thousandfold: small numbers of big things lose to big numbers of small. Division reveals hidden multitudes.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Glass holds ~10^25 molecules; oceans hold ~10^22 glassfuls. Small containers of tiny things outnumber big containers of them — scale inverts intuition.
lessonContent:
Small-of-tiny beats big-of-small.
Division reveals hidden multitudes.
Glassfuls lose to molecules thousandfold.
Intuition inverts across scales reliably.
Share this: drink one ocean-fraction.

title: The Exact Breath
question: Popular accounts claim every breath you take contains exactly one molecule from Julius Caesar's last breath.
correctExplanation: False. Order-of-magnitude math suggests roughly one such molecule per breath — but 'exactly one' overstates estimates built on mixing assumptions. Roughly, not exactly.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The arithmetic gives an order of magnitude (~1), not a guarantee: uneven mixing and uncertain totals forbid exactness. 'Exactly' is where popular science oversells.
lessonContent:
Orders of magnitude are not guarantees.
'Exactly' oversells estimates reliably.
Mixing assumptions carry wide error bars.
Roughly-one differs from exactly-one.
Share this: un-exact one pop fact.

title: The Solar Strand
question: Uncoil the DNA from one cell (~2 meters) across all ~30 trillion body cells and the strand reaches far past the Sun.
correctExplanation: True. Two meters times 30 trillion ≈ 60 billion kilometers — hundreds of Sun-distances. Microscopic lengths times astronomical counts.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Cell-scale DNA multiplied by body-scale cell counts lands in interplanetary ranges: ~6×10^13 meters versus 1.5×10^11 to the Sun. Small times huge equals vast.
lessonContent:
Small times huge equals vast reliably.
Cell scales times body counts astound.
Meters accumulate into astronomical units.
Multiplication humbles intuition fastest.
Share this: strand one body sunward.

title: The Synapse Sky
question: The human cortex holds on the order of 100 trillion synapses — outnumbering the Milky Way's few hundred billion stars.
correctExplanation: True. Synapses (~10^14) beat galactic stars (~10^11) a thousandfold: inner space outpopulates outer, locally.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Count connections, not neurons: 10^14 synapses dwarf 10^11 stars. The richest known network sits behind foreheads, not telescopes.
lessonContent:
Inner space outpopulates outer locally.
Connections outnumber stars thousandfold.
Count links, never just nodes.
Richest networks sit behind foreheads.
Share this: outcount one galaxy inwardly.

title: The Organ Census
question: Microbial cells match human cells exactly one-to-one inside every single organ, from skin to liver to brain.
correctExplanation: False. The rough whole-body parity (Sender 2016) varies wildly by organ: colons teem, blood runs nearly sterile. Global averages never describe locals.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. One-to-one holds approximately body-wide, not organ-wise: guts overflow while blood stays near-empty. Averages describe wholes, never parts.
lessonContent:
Global averages never describe locals.
Guts teem; blood runs sterile.
Whole-body parity varies organ by organ.
Census by district, never by nation.
Share this: district one average tonight.

title: The Tenfold Myth
question: The famous claim that microbes outnumber human cells ten to one was revised by careful counting to roughly one to one.
correctExplanation: True. Sender's 2016 recount replaced the 10:1 myth with ~1:1: better cell counts, humbler ratio. Textbooks update slowly.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The tenfold figure traced to a 1970s rough estimate repeated uncritically for decades. Careful census deflated it tenfold — myths persist past measurements.
lessonContent:
Rough estimates calcify into textbook myths.
Recounts deflate decades-old ratios.
Tenfold errors persist past measurements.
Census carefully before quoting ratios.
Share this: deflate one old ratio.

title: The Third Age
question: At 4.5 billion years, Earth is roughly a third of the universe's 13.8-billion-year age — a comparatively recent construction.
correctExplanation: True. Two-thirds of cosmic history passed before Earth existed: stars lived, died, and seeded the matter we stand on. Recent arrivals, ancient materials.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 4.5 over 13.8 ≈ one third: the universe made galaxies, forged elements, and burned generations of stars first. Planets are latecomers built from elders.
lessonContent:
Planets are latecomers cosmically.
Two-thirds of history predates Earth.
Elders forged our every atom.
Recent arrivals inherit ancient work.
Share this: thank one elder star.

title: The Final Minute
question: Compressed into a cosmic year, all of recorded human history fits inside the final minute before midnight.
correctExplanation: True. Five millennia against 13.8 billion years ≈ eleven seconds: Sagan's calendar puts empires in the last breath of December 31st.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The fraction (~4×10^-7 of a year) lands recorded history within the final minute — writing, pyramids, everything. Calendars compress civilizations into seconds.
lessonContent:
Calendars compress empires into seconds.
Fractions humble recorded history fully.
Midnight nears for all our annals.
Cosmic years dwarf human ones.
Share this: fit history in one minute.

title: The Late Light
question: Light now arriving from Andromeda left its source after anatomically modern humans had already evolved.
correctExplanation: False. Andromeda lies 2.5 million light-years out; Homo sapiens spans ~300,000 years. The light predates humanity eightfold.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Travel time (2.5M years) dwarfs our species' age (~0.3M): arriving photons predate every human eye. Neighbors' mail is ancient history.
lessonContent:
Neighbor mail predates recipients fully.
Travel times dwarf species ages.
Light outruns evolution routinely.
Ancient photons greet young eyes.
Share this: read 2.5-million-year mail.

title: The Ancient Snapshot
question: Every star you see with the naked eye shows light that left years to millennia ago — stargazing is time travel into the past.
correctExplanation: True. Even the nearest stars lag by years; most visible ones by centuries. Night skies are museums admitting free.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Light-travel delays turn every glance backward: Sirius eight years gone, Deneb over a thousand. Present-tense skies show only history.
lessonContent:
Glances travel backward in time.
Museums admit stargazers free nightly.
Present skies show only history.
Delays turn seeing into remembering.
Share this: view one old photograph.

title: The Atomic Etch
question: Leading computer chips now etch features only dozens of atoms wide — transistors approaching countable-atom scales.
correctExplanation: True. Three-nanometer-class features span roughly fifteen silicon atoms: engineering nears atomic grain. Shrinkage ends where atoms begin.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Nanometers translate to atom-counts: ~0.2 nm per atom makes 3 nm about fifteen wide. Moore's march halts at matter's pixels.
lessonContent:
Nanometers translate to atom counts.
Matter's pixels halt shrinkage marches.
Engineering nears countable scales.
Dozens of atoms switch modern worlds.
Share this: count fifteen atoms.

title: The Unique Shuffle
question: A well-shuffled deck almost certainly orders cards in a sequence never before arranged in Earth's entire history (52! ≈ 8×10^67).
correctExplanation: True. Factorial space dwarfs all shuffles ever performed (~10^20 at most): uniqueness is the default. Every riffle makes history.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 52! exceeds atoms-on-Earth scales astronomically: no prior shuffle plausibly repeats. Casinos deal novelties with every hand.
lessonContent:
Factorials dwarf all performed shuffles.
Uniqueness is the default outcome.
Riffles make history every hand.
Astronomical spaces swallow attempts.
Share this: deal one unique history.

title: The Lucky Casino
question: Casino card shuffles routinely repeat exact historical orderings, since dealing volume overcomes even factorial odds.
correctExplanation: False. No dealing volume dents 52!: repeats would need ~10^68 shuffles against ~10^20 performed. Casinos deal firsts, never reruns.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Factorial odds laugh at dealing volumes: 10^67 possibilities versus 10^20 attempts leaves repeats effectively impossible. Volume never overcomes factorials.
lessonContent:
Volumes never overcome factorials.
Firsts, never reruns, leave casinos.
Possibilities dwarf attempts eternally.
Dealing makes history, not repeats.
Share this: deal one more first.

title: The Outnumbered Atoms
question: The number of possible chess games (~10^120) exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe (~10^80).
correctExplanation: True. Shannon's number towers forty orders above atomic counts: game-trees dwarf matter-trees. Possibility outruns substance cosmically.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Branching game paths multiply past every physical inventory: 10^120 versus 10^80. Mind-games exceed world-stuff by cosmic margins.
lessonContent:
Branching outruns inventory cosmically.
Game-trees dwarf matter-trees fully.
Possibility exceeds substance by orders.
Shannon counted past atoms easily.
Share this: play one cosmic game.

title: The Decade Reading
question: Reading the 3 billion letters of one human genome aloud would take the better part of a decade at speaking pace.
correctExplanation: True. Three billion characters at ~10 per second runs ~9.5 years nonstop: genomes are libraries, not pamphlets.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Speaking pace (~10 letters/second) stretches 3×10^9 letters across most of a decade. Reading oneself aloud is a career, not an evening.
lessonContent:
Genomes are libraries, never pamphlets.
Speaking pace spans decades of letters.
Reading oneself takes careers.
Billions humble reading speeds fully.

title: The Starry Forest
question: The Milky Way's stars outnumber all the trees on Earth, since galaxies dwarf any planetary forest.
correctExplanation: False. Earth's ~3 trillion trees beat the galaxy's ~100-400 billion stars roughly tenfold: forests outnumber starfields locally.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Tree censuses (~3×10^12) top stellar counts (~10^11): planets can out-forest galaxies in raw numbers. Galaxies dwarf forests in size, never in count.
lessonContent:
Counts differ from sizes entirely.
Forests outnumber starfields locally.
Trillions of trees beat billions of suns.
Number locally before assuming cosmically.
Share this: count one forest skyward.

title: The Night Shift
question: Red blood cell production shuts down overnight and resumes at dawn, giving marrow a nightly rest like the rest of the body.
correctExplanation: False. Marrow manufactures ~2 million cells per second around the clock: production never sleeps. Factories run night shifts permanently.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Erythropoiesis continues through sleep unabated: millions per second, day and night. Bodies run continuous manufacturing, never bank hours.
lessonContent:
Manufacturing never banks night hours.
Millions per second, asleep or awake.
Marrow works permanent night shifts.
Continuous production beats rest cycles.
Share this: make cells while sleeping.

title: The Billion Beats
question: Mice and elephants — lifespans differing fortyfold — each get roughly a billion heartbeats per lifetime.
correctExplanation: True. Levine's finding: metabolic rate scales so faster hearts buy shorter lives in beats-constant trade. Heartbeats budget lifetimes equally.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Small fast hearts and huge slow ones both spend ~10^9 beats: lifespan trades rate for duration evenly. Billion-beat budgets govern mammals.
lessonContent:
Rate trades duration evenly always.
Billion-beat budgets govern mammals.
Fast small, slow huge: equal totals.
Metabolism prices lifespans in beats.
Share this: spend beats wisely.

title: The Patient Colony
question: One E. coli's unchecked descendants would need many years to outweigh the Earth, since bacteria weigh almost nothing.
correctExplanation: False. Twenty-minute doublings hit Earth-mass in under two days: exponentials mock 'almost nothing' fast. Years overestimates by hundredfold.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Doubling math: ~132 doublings at 20 minutes ≈ 44 hours to planetary mass. 'Almost nothing' times exponential equals everything quickly.
lessonContent:
Exponentials mock tiny starting masses.
Doubling counts beat intuition always.
Hours, never years, reach planetary mass.
'Nothing' compounds into everything.
Share this: double one penny mentally.

title: The Doubled Penny
question: A penny doubled daily for a month ends above ten million dollars — beating a flat million-dollar gift.
correctExplanation: True. 2^30 pennies ≈ $10.7 million: exponentials cross linear gifts mid-month and never look back. Patience outperforms principal.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Doubling compounds past millions around day 28: flat gifts lead early, exponentials win late. Never bet against thirty doublings.
lessonContent:
Exponentials cross linear gifts mid-race.
Patience outperforms principal reliably.
Thirty doublings beat flat millions.
Never bet against compounding streaks.
Share this: double one penny daily.

title: The Earthborn Atoms
question: Nearly all the atoms in your body formed together with the Earth itself, 4.5 billion years ago.
correctExplanation: False. Hydrogen dates to the Big Bang; heavy elements to earlier stars: most atoms predate Earth by billions. Bodies are older than their planet.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Stellar nucleosynthesis predates solar systems: carbon, oxygen, iron all cooked in prior suns. Earth assembled elders, never newborns.
lessonContent:
Bodies predate their planets fully.
Elders forged every heavy atom.
Earth assembled ancients, never newborns.
Stardust is literal, not lyrical.
